The experiment. All three products ran on the same twelve invented sessions between a user, Sam, and an assistant (the parent frameworks root's four sessions extended to twelve; invented, assistant turns are fixed text so every system saw exactly the same history; about 1,400 tokens in all, so the full history fits and is an honest upper bound), then answered 25 questions in LongMemEval's five abilities, asked "on" 6 October 2026. Two measurements per answer: did the evidence words reach the prompt (no model needed), and was the answer right (keyword rules per question; an abstention question passes when the answer says it does not know or corrects the false premise; every answer was also read by hand). Writers and readers are Claude Haiku 4.5 and a local Qwen3-4B on Apple M1 Pro. A demonstration of mechanisms, not a benchmark MEASURED.

What the table says. Pasting the whole history scored 23 of 25; the best memory, the paper loop with a Haiku writer, 24; Mem0 2.2.1 22; Graphiti 15, because only 14 of 21 answers' evidence reached the prompt; Letta's own loop 4, though its notes pasted whole gave 21: its write side worked and its read side did not (it searched on 5 of 25 questions). With no memory at all, 4. Swap the writer for the 4B model and the same designs lose facts: the paper loop fell to 19 and Graphiti to 5.

Claude figures are the CLI's API-price equivalent at Haiku 4.5 list prices; local-model figures are tokens and seconds on a shared M1 Pro, comparable only with each other. Mem0's input is dominated by its extraction prompt (7,924 tokens with the Qwen tokenizer, over the shared local server's limit, which is why the library's writes used Haiku). Graphiti made 71 calls for 12 episodes: two is the minimum per episode (entities, then facts), and every new fact that resembles an old one costs another resolve_edge call (26 of them here). Letta has no separate search step: its 25 answers took 36 model calls inside its own loop.

break-even sessions ≈ write cost per session / (history tokens saved per answer × answers per session × input price)

At this size pasting everything is cheaper than any memory layer for a long time. The vendors' own numbers say the same at their scale: Mem0's paper puts full context at 26,031 tokens per LOCOMO conversation against 1,764 for Mem0, Zep's about 115K against 1.6K on LongMemEval; the saving appears only once history is tens of thousands of tokens and is read many times.

Every published benchmark number for these products, with its runner

No benchmark was rerun here. LOCOMO (Maharana et al., arXiv 2402.17753, Feb 2024) is long two-person chats scored by an LLM judge (the "J score"); the paper describes 50 conversations of about 300 turns and 9K tokens, up to 35 sessions; its public release has 10 conversations, 1,986 questions, and 444 of the 446 adversarial questions have no reference answer, so every product evaluation drops that category; it has no knowledge-update questions. LongMemEval (arXiv 2410.10813, ICLR 2025) has 500 questions over histories of about 115K tokens (setting S) or about 500 sessions and 1.5M tokens (M); counts in the released file: temporal 133, multi-session 133, knowledge update 78, single-session user 70, assistant 56, preference 30, with 30 abstention variants. DMR, MemGPT's test, has 5 short sessions per conversation, which fit in a window. MemoryAgentBench (UCSD, arXiv 2507.05257) is independent.

The same product, Zep, scored 58.44%, 65.99%, 75.14% and up to 80.32% on LOCOMO depending on who configured it, the retrieval template, how many results were retrieved and how one category was counted. Ask five things of any memory benchmark claim: who ran it; does the whole history fit the answer model's window (then full context is the baseline to beat, and it often wins); which answer and judge models; how many memories were retrieved per question; which product version. Sources read 6 Oct 2026, quotes in src/memory_layers/inputs/research_claims.md.
